title: Vector Databases
summary: Vector databases store millions of embeddings and retrieve the most similar ones in milliseconds using approximate nearest neighbor indexes. They add persistence, metadata filtering, and scalability to semantic search. Every production RAG system rel
content:
# Vector Databases ##### 47 seconds per query, and the RAM ran out The Ahmedabad team from Day 33 fixed their chunking and shipped. Then they added the rest of the corpus — three years of policy documents, claim precedents, and circulars. 1.4 million chunks. Their brute-force search stopped working in two ways at once. **Speed:** every query computed 1.4 million dot products against 768-dimensional vectors. On their server, 47 seconds. Users abandoned the page at four. **Memory:** 1.4M × 768 × 4 bytes = 4.3 GB of float32, plus the chunk text, loaded into RAM on every process restart. Their container had 4 GB. And a third problem they had not anticipated: every deploy re-embedded the entire corpus, taking 40 minutes and about ₹4,000 in API calls. They moved to a vector database. Query latency dropped to 12 milliseconds, memory usage to under 500 MB, and restarts became instant because the index was on disk. **A vector database is what turns semantic search from a notebook demo into a system.** Three things it gives you: approximate nearest neighbour indexes for speed, persistence so you embed once, and metadata filtering so you can search *within* a subset. ##### The brute-force wall Exact search is O(n·d) per query — n documents, d dimensions. ```python import numpy as np, time for n in [1_000, 100_000, 1_400_000]: E = np.random.randn(n, 768).astype(np.float32) E /= np.linalg.norm(E, axis=1, keepdims=True) q = np.random.randn(768).astype(np.float32); q /= np.linalg.norm(q) t0 = time.perf_counter() top = np.argsort(-(E @ q))[:10] print(f"n={n:>9,} {(time.perf_counter()-t0)*1000:>8.1f} ms " f"{E.nbytes/1e9:.2f} GB") ``` Brute force is fine up to roughly 50,000 vectors — genuinely fine, and you should not add infrastructure before you need it. Past a few hundred thousand it stops being viable. The escape is to **give up exactness**. Approximate nearest neighbour search returns the right answers 95–99% of the time, thousands of times faster. For retrieval, where the "correct" chunk is a matter of judgement anyway, that trade is almost always worth it. ##### HNSW Hierarchical Navigable Small World (Malkov & Yashunin, 2016) is the index most vector databases use by default, and the intuition is worth having. Imagine navigating India by air. You do not check every one of 700 towns. You fly Mumbai → Bengaluru (long hop, top layer), then Bengaluru → Mysuru (medium hop), then drive to the specific address (bottom layer). Each layer is denser and shorter-range than the one above. ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph L2["Layer 2 — sparse, long jumps"] A2["●"] --- B2["●"] end subgraph L1["Layer 1 — medium density"] A1["●"] --- B1["●"] --- C1["●"] --- D1["●"] end subgraph L0["Layer 0 — all vectors, short links"] A0["●"] --- B0["●"] --- C0["●"] --- D0["●"] --- E0["●"] --- F0["●"] end A2 -.descend.-> B1 B1 -.descend.-> C0 Q["Query enters
at the top"] --> A2 C0 --> R["Nearest neighbours found
in O(log n) hops"] ``` Search enters at the sparse top layer, greedily walks toward the query, descends a layer, repeats. Complexity is roughly **O(log n)** instead of O(n). **The parameters you will actually set:** | Parameter | Meaning | Typical | Trade-off | |---|---|---|---| | `M` | Links per node | 16–64 | Higher = better recall, more memory | | `ef_construction` | Candidates during build | 100–500 | Higher = better index, slower build | | `ef_search` | Candidates during query | 50–200 | Higher = better recall, slower query | `ef_search` is tunable **at query time**, which is genuinely useful: run at 50 for interactive search and 200 for an offline evaluation job, using the same index. Other index types worth recognising: **Flat** (exact brute force — correct default under ~50K vectors), **IVF** (cluster the space, search only nearby clusters), and **PQ / product quantization** (compress vectors to save memory, at some accuracy cost). IVF+PQ is what you use at hundreds of millions of vectors. ##### Choosing a vector database | | Chroma | FAISS | Qdrant | Pinecone | pgvector | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Type | Embedded DB | Library | Server/cloud | Managed cloud | Postgres extension | | Setup | `pip install` | `pip install` | Docker | API key | Postgres extension | | Persistence | ✓ built in | Manual save/load | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | | Metadata filtering | ✓ | ✗ (do it yourself) | ✓ excellent | ✓ | ✓ SQL | | Scale | ~1M | 1B+ | 100M+ | Billions | ~10M | | Ops burden | None | None | You run it | None | You already have it | | Cost | Free | Free | Free / hosted | Paid | Free | **Practical guidance:** - **Learning and prototyping** → Chroma. It is a `pip install`, persists to disk, and handles metadata. - **Maximum speed, no metadata needed** → FAISS. It is a library, not a database — the fastest option and the most manual. - **Production, self-hosted** → Qdrant or Weaviate. - **Production, do not want to run infrastructure** → Pinecone. - **You already run Postgres** → pgvector. Seriously consider this; one fewer system to operate is worth a lot, and it handles millions of vectors fine. That last point deserves emphasis. Teams routinely add a dedicated vector database for 40,000 chunks when a `vector` column in their existing Postgres would work perfectly. Do not add infrastructure you do not need. ##### Chroma in practice ```python import chromadb from chromadb.utils import embedding_functions client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./vectordb") # ← persists to disk embed_fn = embedding_functions.SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction( model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2" ) collection = client.get_or_create_collection( name="policy_docs", embedding_function=embed_fn, metadata={"hnsw:space": "cosine", "hnsw:M": 32, "hnsw:construction_ef": 200}, ) # Upsert — insert or update by ID collection.upsert( ids=["pol-2026-001-c0", "pol-2026-001-c1", "pol-2024-018-c0"], documents=[ "Reimbursement for treatment at non-network hospitals requires prior authorisation...", "Claims must be submitted within 30 days of discharge along with original bills...", "The 2024 circular revised the sub-limit for room rent to Rs 5,000 per day...", ], metadatas=[ {"doc_id": "pol-2026-001", "year": 2026, "type": "policy", "state": "Gujarat"}, {"doc_id": "pol-2026-001", "year": 2026, "type": "policy", "state": "Gujarat"}, {"doc_id": "pol-2024-018", "year": 2024, "type": "circular", "state": "all"}, ], ) results = collection.query( query_texts=["Can I claim for a non-network hospital?"], n_results=3, include=["documents", "metadatas", "distances"], ) for doc, meta, dist in zip(results["documents"][0], results["metadatas"][0], results["distances"][0]): print(f"[sim {1 - dist:.3f}] ({meta['doc_id']}) {doc[:90]}...") ``` **Note `upsert` rather than `add`.** Re-running an ingestion script with `add` creates duplicates; `upsert` updates in place. Use deterministic IDs derived from source and chunk index, and re-ingestion becomes idempotent. **Chroma returns distances, not similarities.** For the cosine space, `similarity = 1 - distance`. Getting this backwards and sorting the wrong way is a genuinely common bug. ##### Metadata filtering This is the capability that most distinguishes a vector database from a plain index, and it is used constantly in production. ```python # Only 2026 policies collection.query( query_texts=["room rent sub-limit"], n_results=5, where={"year": 2026}, ) # Compound conditions collection.query( query_texts=["claim submission deadline"], n_results=5, where={"$and": [ {"type": {"$eq": "policy"}}, {"year": {"$gte": 2025}}, {"state": {"$in": ["Gujarat", "all"]}}, ]}, ) # Full-text condition on the document body collection.query( query_texts=["authorisation process"], n_results=5, where_document={"$contains": "prior authorisation"}, ) ``` Real uses: **access control** (only return documents this user may see), **recency** (only the current policy version), **language**, **source**, and **tenant isolation** in a multi-customer product. That access-control case is not a nice-to-have. Without metadata filtering, a RAG system over internal documents will happily retrieve HR salary data for an intern's query. Filtering at the retrieval layer is your enforcement point. **Two ways databases implement filtering**, and it matters: - **Pre-filtering** — narrow by metadata first, then search. Exact, but can be slow if the filter is expensive. - **Post-filtering** — search first, then discard non-matching. Fast, but if only 2% of your corpus matches the filter, your top-100 might contain zero valid results. Qdrant and Weaviate do filtered HNSW traversal, which handles restrictive filters well. If you use post-filtering with a narrow filter, raise `n_results` substantially to compensate. ##### FAISS FAISS is a library, not a database. No metadata, no persistence layer, no server — just extremely fast vector search. ```python import faiss import numpy as np import pickle embeddings = np.load("embeddings.npy").astype("float32") # (n, 768) faiss.normalize_L2(embeddings) # for cosine d = embeddings.shape[1] if len(embeddings) < 50_000: index = faiss.IndexFlatIP(d) # exact, inner product else: index = faiss.IndexHNSWFlat(d, 32) # HNSW, M=32 index.hnsw.efConstruction = 200 index.hnsw.efSearch = 64 index.add(embeddings) print("indexed:", index.ntotal) q = model.encode(["non-network hospital claim"], normalize_embeddings=True) scores, ids = index.search(q.astype("float32"), k=5) faiss.write_index(index, "policy.faiss") with open("policy_meta.pkl", "wb") as f: pickle.dump(chunk_metadata, f) # you manage metadata yourself ``` That last block is the trade: FAISS gives you speed and requires you to maintain the parallel metadata store, handle persistence, and implement filtering by hand. ##### Scaling considerations **Memory.** HNSW keeps the index in RAM. Estimate roughly: ```python def hnsw_memory_gb(n_vectors, dims, M=32, dtype_bytes=4): vectors = n_vectors * dims * dtype_bytes graph = n_vectors * M * 2 * 8 # bidirectional links, 8 bytes each return (vectors + graph) / 1e9 print(f"{hnsw_memory_gb(1_400_000, 768):.2f} GB") # 4.60 GB print(f"{hnsw_memory_gb(1_400_000, 384):.2f} GB") # 2.87 GB ``` **Dimension reduction is the cheapest lever.** Moving from 768 to 384 dimensions halves memory and roughly halves query time. OpenAI's `text-embedding-3` models support **Matryoshka truncation** — you can simply take the first N dimensions and renormalise, losing very little quality: ```python emb = client.embeddings.create(model="text-embedding-3-large", input=texts, dimensions=512) ``` **Quantization.** Storing vectors as int8 rather than float32 cuts memory 4× for a small recall cost. Binary quantization goes to 32× and is used with a rescoring pass. **Other scaling notes:** batch your upserts (1,000 at a time, not one by one), rebuild indexes during off-hours if your database requires it, and shard by tenant or time period when a single index gets unwieldy. ##### Common mistakes - **Adding a vector database for 20,000 chunks.** Brute-force NumPy or pgvector is fine. - **Using `add` instead of `upsert`**, creating duplicates on re-ingestion. - **Confusing distance with similarity** and sorting the wrong way. - **Not persisting**, re-embedding on every restart — 40 minutes and ₹4,000. - **Ignoring metadata filtering** and leaking documents across access boundaries. - **Post-filtering with a very restrictive filter**, returning nothing useful. - **`ef_search` left at the default** when recall matters. - **Querying with a different embedding model** than the one used to index. - **No index versioning**, so changing the embedding model silently corrupts results. - **Storing full document text in metadata**, bloating the index. - **Never measuring recall against exact search** to verify your ANN settings are sane. ##### Hands-on: migrate and measure Your practical task loads documents into Chroma or FAISS, queries them, and filters by metadata. Attach at least three metadata fields — source, date, and a category — and then run the same query with and without a filter. Seeing the result set change based on metadata is what makes the access-control use case concrete. The mini project migrates your Day 33 engine to a vector database with persistence and filters. Keep the same interface (`add_documents`, `search`) so the swap is invisible to calling code — that is good design practice and it makes the before/after comparison clean. Then measure: index build time, query latency, and memory, before and after. Restart your process and confirm the index loads from disk rather than re-embedding. The assignment compares two vector databases on setup, speed, and features. Chroma versus FAISS is the natural pairing because they represent opposite philosophies — batteries-included database versus bare-metal library. **Measure recall against exact brute force**, not just speed: build a Flat index as ground truth, then check what fraction of the true top-10 your HNSW index returns. If recall is 0.94, you now know precisely what your speedup cost. ##### Key takeaways - **Brute-force search is fine to about 50,000 vectors** — do not add infrastructure before you need it, and consider pgvector before a dedicated database. - **HNSW trades exactness for O(log n) search** by navigating a layered graph from sparse long hops down to dense short ones, and `ef_search` tunes recall at query time. - **Persistence is why you use a database**: embed once, restart instantly, stop paying to re-embed on every deploy. - **Metadata filtering is the production-critical feature** — it enforces access control, recency, and tenant isolation at the retrieval layer. - **Measure recall against exact search.** ANN is approximate by definition, and knowing you are at 0.94 rather than assuming 1.0 is what makes the trade-off an engineering decision.
